issues.title: How reliable are LLMs at mapping malware/threat behavior to MITRE ATT&CK techniques (TTP mapping)?
open_questions: Does the CTI-ATE F1 ceiling of 0.64 (src-0002, mid-2024 models) generalize to the newer/larger models evaluated in CyberSOCEval (src-0005, 2025-era), which did not report a directly comparable ATT&CK-technique-extraction metric?
Is there a human-analyst baseline F1 for ATT&CK technique extraction to contextualize whether 0.64 is 'close to human' or far below it?

PARTIALLY ANSWERED cycle 16, and for the generic case the answer is NO -- fine-tuning made this sub-task WORSE, not better. src-0007's Table 4 gives ATT&CK TTP identification precision/recall of 0.2787/0.2270 for GPT-4o falling to 0.2387/0.1846 for the fine-tuned GPT-4o, and 0.1771/0.1414 for fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini, against 0.3480/0.1759 for o3-mini. All nine of those figures were re-verified verbatim by cycle 15's G2 and matched exactly to four decimal places. This directly matches src-0001's finding that fine-tuning can actively degrade CTI sub-tasks rather than 'partially improve' them. STILL OPEN AS LITERALLY POSED: src-0007's fine-tuning is general task fine-tuning, not fine-tuning specifically on ATT&CK-technique-extraction data, so whether a targeted ATT&CK fine-tune would behave differently is untested by any source in this base.

candidate_resolutions.summary: MITRE ATT&CK technique extraction from threat/malware text remains a hard, unsolved sub-task for LLMs: best-in-class F1 was only 0.6388 (GPT-4-turbo) on CTIBench's CTI-ATE task, far below the ~71-72% accuracy the same models reach on knowledge-recall tasks. Newer, larger 2025-era models improve on general malware-analysis/threat-intel-reasoning benchmarks per scaling laws, but test-time-scaling 'reasoning' gains that help coding/math do not transfer to these cybersecurity reasoning tasks, so the ATT&CK-mapping gap specifically has not been shown to close with the latest model generation.

ADDED cycle 16 by T2, discharging carry-forward [2] which was cited in cycles 10 and 13 rationales but never attached to the graph. A third independent source now measures ATT&CK technique mapping and it lands FAR BELOW CTIBench's already-low ceiling. src-0007 (CyberThreat-Eval; Microsoft Research/Microsoft/HKUST, Mar 2026), on expert-annotated material drawn from a real company's daily CTI workflow, reports MITRE ATT&CK TTP identification precision/recall of 0.2787/0.2270 (GPT-4o), 0.3480/0.1759 (o3-mini), 0.2387/0.1846 (fine-tuned GPT-4o) and 0.1771/0.1414 (fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini) -- against src-0002's CTI-ATE best-model F1 ceiling of 0.6388. THIS IS NOT A CONTRADICTION WITH src-0002 and no G3 entry was opened: different benchmark, different corpus, and a different metric decomposition (precision and recall separately, no F1), and real production material proving harder than a curated benchmark is the expected direction rather than a conflicting one. What src-0007 adds is twofold. (a) INDEPENDENCE: its authors are unaffiliated with CTIBench's and with PRISM/LANCE's, so the hardness of ATT&CK mapping is no longer resting on one team's benchmark design. (b) A WITHIN-TABLE CONTROL that cross-benchmark synthesis cannot supply: the identical models, on the identical corpus, through the identical harness, reach 0.8240-0.8846 precision on mechanical IoC extraction in the same table, so the ATT&CK deficit cannot be attributed to corpus difficulty or prompt harness quality. Provenance note: every figure quoted here was re-verified verbatim against the source by cycle 15's G2, exact to four decimal places, with no discrepancy.

issues.title: How reliable is LLM-assisted extraction of mechanical indicators of compromise (IPs, domains, URLs, hashes) from threat reports?
open_questions: STILL OPEN, BUT SHARPENED (cycle 9): no direct replication or critique of LANCE/PRISM exists -- cycle 6 searched for one and cycle 9 searched again over a wider net (see logs/cycle-009.md for exact queries), and 2603.09452 and 2605.06910 do not cite arXiv 2506.11325 at all. What now exists instead is an independent measurement of a DIFFERENT system on a DIFFERENT corpus (src-0007, vanilla LLM IoC extraction, precision 0.82-0.88) sitting ~10-15 points below LANCE's 97.6% F1. The live question is no longer 'has anyone replicated LANCE' (no) but 'is the gap between 97.6% and 0.82-0.88 explained by LANCE's regex pre-filter + human-validation loop, by corpus difficulty, or by the metric difference (F1 vs precision-only)?' Answering it needs a head-to-head: run LANCE on CyberThreat-Eval's IoC set, or run a vanilla LLM on PRISM.

Does the result generalize beyond the 4 indicator types tested (IPs, domains, URLs, hashes) to e.g. registry keys, mutexes, YARA/Sigma rules? Cycle 9 note: src-0007 does NOT extend the coverage -- its ground truth is described as 'file hashes, IP addresses, or domain names'. Two independent benchmarks now both confine themselves to the same small family of network/file indicators, which suggests the field has not measured the harder indicator types at all rather than that they were measured and found comparable.

How much of LANCE's gain over IoC Searcher/AlienVault OTX/VirusTotal comes from the LLM component specifically vs. the regex pre-filtering and human-validation loop around it? Cycle 9 gives the first indirect evidence: src-0007's Table 4 is explicitly headed 'Vanilla LLMs' and a bare LLM there reaches only 0.82-0.85 precision on expert-annotated real-world data, which is consistent with (though it does not prove) the LLM component alone not being what delivers high-90s performance. Confounded by corpus and metric differences.

NEW (cycle 9): src-0007 reports precision only for IoC extraction, with no recall or F1 and no stated reason. Recall is exactly the axis on which the legacy baselines were weakest in src-0003, so the comparison is currently one-sided. The authors state code is available on GitHub and HuggingFace -- can recall/F1 be recovered from the released benchmark to make a like-for-like comparison with src-0003's F1?

NEW (cycle 9): src-0008 shows LLM recovery of plaintext indicators from code is ~100% but collapses to ~0-1% under XOR/AES-256 concealment. Report-based extraction has never been evaluated under an adversarial threat model at all -- if report authors or adversaries defang/encode indicators (a routine practice in published reporting), does extraction accuracy degrade similarly? No source measures this.

candidate_resolutions.summary: For narrow, mechanical IoC extraction (as opposed to open-ended CTI reasoning), a hybrid regex+LLM+human-validation pipeline (LANCE) reached 97.6% F1 against the manually-validated PRISM benchmark, substantially outperforming legacy tools (IoC Searcher+whitelist 76%, AlienVault OTX 72%, VirusTotal@threshold=1 86%) and also improving downstream analyst speed (43% less annotation time) and downstream model training data quality (+6% F1). This is a single-study result from the benchmark's own authors, not yet independently replicated.

ADDED cycle 9. A second, fully independent measurement of LLM IoC extraction from real-world CTI material now exists: CyberThreat-Eval (src-0007; Microsoft Research/Microsoft/HKUST, Mar 2026), an expert-annotated benchmark built from a production CTI workflow covering 1310 IoCs, reports vanilla-LLM extraction precision of 0.8240 (GPT-4o), 0.8503 (o3-mini), 0.8846 (fine-tuned GPT-4o) and 0.6944 (fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini). Read narrowly, this establishes that a bare LLM prompted to extract indicators from real analyst-workflow material errs on roughly 1 in 6 of the indicators it emits -- materially short of the near-solved impression left by src-0003's 97.6% F1, and short of even the 86% VirusTotal@threshold=1 baseline src-0003 reports. It does NOT refute src-0003, because it measures a different system (no regex pre-filter, no human validation loop), on a different corpus, with a different metric (precision only; no recall or F1 given). See contradiction ctr-0001, opened this cycle rather than resolved either way.

ADDED cycle 9, deliberately weak status. Candidate synthesis: the reliability of mechanical IoC extraction is set mainly by the scaffolding around the model (regex pre-filtering, whitelisting, human validation) rather than by the LLM itself, which is why src-0003's scaffolded pipeline reports 97.6% F1 while src-0007's 'Vanilla LLMs' reach 0.82-0.88 precision and src-0008 finds an unscaffolded LLM recovers plaintext indicators ~100% of the time but is defeated entirely by encryption it has no tooling for. This is a plausible reading of three sources that were never designed to be compared, and no source tests it directly -- it is recorded as proposed so a later cycle can attack it, NOT as a finding.

issues.title: Beyond raw accuracy, are LLM-generated CTI outputs consistent across repeated queries and well-calibrated in stated confidence?
open_questions: Table 6's calibration numbers were captured for gpt4o only across a handful of entity types (Campaign, APT, CVE extraction; CVE, attack-vector generation) -- do gemini-1.5-pro-latest and mistral-large-2 show the same fine-tuning-can-worsen-calibration pattern, or is it gpt4o-specific?

None of src-0001's 3 tested models (gpt4o, gemini-1.5-pro-latest, mistral-large-2) overlap with src-0002's (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, Gemini-1.5, LLAMA3-70B/8B) or src-0005's model lists -- would the consistency/calibration findings replicate on the specific models shown to struggle with ATT&CK mapping and attribution in those benchmarks?

Does the multi-dimensional reliability framing (accuracy + consistency + calibration) proposed in src-0001 apply equally across the other CTI sub-tasks measured in src-0002/src-0005 (MCQ, RCM, ATE, TAA, malware analysis), or was it only measured in src-0001's own information-extraction/-generation evaluation setting?

Fine-tuning and few-shot were both shown to sometimes worsen accuracy and calibration (e.g. gpt4o APT-extraction P/R 0.87->0.68 after fine-tuning; CVE-generation ECE 0.15->0.91) rather than merely 'partially improving' as the abstract states -- is this degradation specific to small fine-tuning dataset size / overfitting, or a more general risk for CTI fine-tuning regardless of data volume?

candidate_resolutions.summary: Reliability for CTI cannot be reduced to accuracy alone: on a 350-real-report evaluation, tested LLMs were both inconsistent across repeated/paraphrased queries and overconfident relative to their actual correctness, and this did not resolve with few-shot learning or fine-tuning (only partial improvement across all three paradigms tested). Exact per-model numeric scores are not yet captured in our knowledge base and are needed before this can be scored as strongly (vs. qualitatively) supported.

Full-text retrieval (cycle 3) confirms and sharpens the above with concrete numbers. The 3 tested models were gpt4o, gemini-1.5-pro-latest, and mistral-large-2. Consistency (10-re-prompt bootstrapped confidence intervals) was tight for mechanical information-extraction (max CI width 0.02) but notably wider for open-ended information-generation (max CI width 0.06). Calibration (ECE/Brier, gpt4o) was substantially worse for generation than extraction sub-tasks, and critically, fine-tuning and few-shot prompting often WORSENED both accuracy and calibration rather than uniformly 'partially improving' them -- e.g. gpt4o APT-extraction precision/recall fell from 0.87 (zero-shot) to 0.68 (fine-tuned), and CVE-generation ECE rose from 0.15 to 0.91 after fine-tuning. This refines the cycle-2 resolution: the unreliability is not just persistent across paradigms -- more training examples or fine-tuning can actively degrade both accuracy and calibration on some CTI sub-tasks.

ADDED cycle 15 by a T1 collect, status PROPOSED and deliberately not promoted -- READ THE SCOPE LIMIT BEFORE USING IT. This issue sat at score 2 from cycle 3 to cycle 15 for one reason: both candidate_resolutions above cite src-0001 and nothing else, and single-source support is a 2 by rubric. Four independent sources now measure the consistency/calibration/abstention axes on SECURITY tasks, none by src-0001's team, none on CTI material. (1) CALIBRATION: src-0013 (Siddiq/Rahman/Santos, ICSME 2026) is the first non-src-0001 source in this base reporting ECE and Brier on a security task -- GPT-4o-mini ECE 0.456-0.481, Qwen3-Coder-Next 0.408-0.421, Gemini-2.0-Flash 0.247-0.263 -- and independently reproduces src-0001's most counter-intuitive result, that an intervention meant to help can worsen calibration: moving from a controlled benchmark to a realistic repository-level setting raised ECE for every model (GPT-4o-mini 0.411->0.697, Gemini 0.161->0.721) and architectural gating helped on the controlled benchmark while degrading the realistic one. (2) INSTABILITY UNDER REPEATED IDENTICAL QUERY, src-0001's own method: src-0016 (Snyk VulnBench JS 1.0) ran each task five times with code, prompt and harness held constant and found 134/158 reference-matched findings recurred in all five runs while 80/161 unmatched findings appeared in only one of five -- a grounded-stable / volunteered-unstable split that parallels src-0001's extraction-vs-generation CI-width divide (0.02 vs 0.06). (3) PROMPT SENSITIVITY AND ABSTENTION: src-0014 (PromptAudit) fixes dataset/decoding/parsing and varies only prompting strategy, finding cross-strategy F1 ranges from 0.398 (Gemma) down to 0.103 (Mistral) and that self-consistency collapses coverage to 24.04-60.85%. (4) UNDER-REFUSAL: src-0015 (OpenSec) finds frontier IR agents over-trigger (GPT-5.2 100% containment at 82.5% FP) and locates the defect precisely -- 'the calibration gap is not in detection but in restraint' -- the same shape as src-0007's triage asymmetry. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT DO. It DOES establish that consistency failure, overconfidence and under-refusal are not artefacts of one team, one paper, one model family or one evaluation harness, and it supplies the base's first abstention data. It DOES NOT replicate src-0001 on CTI: every one of the four measures a security-adjacent task (secure code generation, CVE-code vulnerability detection, JavaScript SAST review, simulated incident response), NOT IoC extraction, TTP mapping, attribution or threat-report drafting. So open_question (ii) -- would the findings replicate on src-0002's and src-0005's model lists on CTI tasks -- REMAINS FULLY OPEN, and none of the four tests a model from src-0001's, src-0002's or src-0005's lists. A T4 scoring this issue must decide explicitly whether cross-domain corroboration on the same failure mode counts toward multi-source support or whether the domain gap holds it at 2; that judgement has not been made and this entry does not make it.

SCOPE RULING, made by T2 at cycle 16 and recorded here so that no future cycle re-litigates it. THE QUESTION cycle 15's T1 raised and correctly refused to answer: it added four independent sources (src-0013, src-0014, src-0015, src-0016) measuring consistency, calibration and abstention on SECURITY tasks, and asked whether cross-domain corroboration of the same failure mode counts toward multi-source support for this issue, or whether the domain gap holds it at single-source. THE RULING IS THAT THE DOMAIN GAP HOLDS. This issue's scope stays anchored to CTI, and the two candidate_resolutions above -- the only ones making a claim about CTI material -- remain single-source (src-0001) for scoring purposes. REASONING, three grounds. (a) Every one of the four measures a security-ADJACENT task -- secure code generation, CVE-code vulnerability detection, JavaScript SAST review, simulated incident response -- and none measures IoC extraction, TTP mapping, attribution or threat-report drafting, which are the tasks this topic is scoped to. (b) Not one tests a model from src-0001's, src-0002's or src-0005's lists; the model overlap is empty, so open_questions (i) and (ii) are untouched by them and must NOT be marked answered. (c) This base's own precedent for admitting a security-adjacent source is src-0008 (JavaScript obfuscation), which was admitted WITH an explicit scope gap and was never treated as a replication of the CTI work; ruling the other way here would retroactively change what that precedent meant. WHAT IS NEVERTHELESS ESTABLISHED, and it is not nothing: the MECHANISM -- output instability under identical or perturbed input, systematic overconfidence, and under-refusal -- is robust across four unrelated teams, four methods, four corpora and roughly fifteen models, so it is not an artefact of one paper, one team or one model family; and two of src-0001's most fragile-looking sub-findings are independently echoed by different mechanisms (an intervention intended to help WORSENING calibration: src-0013's repository-level ECE rising 0.411 to 0.697 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.161 to 0.721 for Gemini-2.0-Flash, and src-0014's adaptive-CoT reducing recall for every model, e.g. Gemma 0.420 to 0.057; and GROUNDED-OUTPUT-STABLE versus VOLUNTEERED-OUTPUT-UNSTABLE: src-0016's 134 of 158 reference-matched findings recurring in all five identical repetitions against 80 of 161 unmatched findings appearing in only one of five, paralleling src-0001's extraction-vs-generation CI widths of 0.02 vs 0.06). That is a claim about SECURITY-TASK LLM RELIABILITY GENERALLY. It is held here as context for the CTI claim, not as support for it. CONSEQUENCE FOR A T4: score this issue on its CTI candidates. A T4 may overrule this scope ruling, but if it does it must say so explicitly and give its reason -- what it must not do is silently count the four as multi-source support for a CTI claim. NO SCORE IS SET HERE; scoring is T4's work and this entry deliberately does not perform it. TWO THINGS REMAIN UNCHANGED AND SHOULD NOT BE FORGOTTEN: this base still has no non-src-0001 source measuring consistency AND calibration together, and per carry-forward [20] src-0013's and src-0014's numbers are single-pass fetches whose results tables have never been pulled whole, with src-0013 additionally carrying an unreconciled internal discrepancy (False Trust for GPT-4o-mini given as 33.9% in one section and as rising from 16.9% to 83.2% in another) -- those two figures must not be quoted together until a G2 pulls that table.

issues.title: How large is the gap between 'plausible-sounding' and 'factually correct' LLM threat-actor attribution?
open_questions: PARTIALLY INFORMED cycle 16, still open. The question asks whether the plausible-vs-correct gap measured on 2024-era models (CTI-TAA in CTIBench) narrows for later models. src-0007 supplies the first later-generation datapoint on threat-actor content and it cuts BOTH ways: o3-mini (a 2025 reasoning model) scores 3.964/3.656/2.968 on the Relevance/Accuracy/Attribution rubric against GPT-4o's 1.547/1.528/1.140 on the same task and corpus, so a newer model is far better -- but 2.968/5 on Attribution is still the lowest of that model's own content scores, and the rubric is not commensurable with CTIBench's plausible-vs-correct percentage split, so this does not answer the question as posed. What is still missing is any source reporting a plausible-vs-correct attribution split for a post-2024 model.
Is attribution error correlated with how well-documented a threat actor group is (e.g. major APTs with abundant public reporting vs. obscure/emerging groups)?

Did ENISA's APT29/'Midnight Blizzard' naming-convention hallucination (src-0004) contribute to, or correlate with, the kind of plausible-but-wrong attribution measured quantitatively in src-0002, or is it a distinct hallucination sub-type (citation/naming fabrication vs. attribution judgment)?

candidate_resolutions.summary: On CTI-TAA (threat-actor attribution over 50 real reports), every one of the 5 tested models' 'plausible-sounding' attribution rate substantially exceeds its 'correct' attribution rate (e.g. GPT-4-turbo: 86% plausible vs 52% correct; Gemini-1.5: 74% vs 38%), a quantified benchmark instance of the broader confident-but-wrong pattern also observed qualitatively in src-0001 and, in a production setting, in src-0004's ENISA incident (misattributed threat-actor naming convention published in an official report).

ADDED cycle 16 by T2, discharging carry-forward [19]. This is a third independent quantitative datapoint on threat-actor attribution quality, alongside src-0002's plausible-vs-correct split and src-0004's ENISA misattribution, and it was invisible to every cycle before 15 because it sits in rows of src-0007's Table 4 that no cycle had pulled until cycle 15's G2 asked for the table whole. On src-0007's threat-intelligence drafting task, the 1-5 rubric scores for 'Content: Threat Actor' are GPT-4o 1.547 Relevance / 1.528 Accuracy / 1.140 Attribution against o3-mini 3.964 / 3.656 / 2.968 -- roughly a 2.6x model gap on the same task, corpus and rubric. THE LOAD-BEARING PART IS THE WITHIN-TABLE CONTRAST, not the model gap: the same GPT-4o scores 3.686 / 3.458 / 3.612 on 'Content: Root Cause' in the same table, so its 1.140 on threat-actor attribution is a deficit specific to attribution rather than a general inability to draft. That is the same shape as src-0002's finding by a different measurement instrument. CAVEATS, RECORDED AT ENTRY, DO NOT STRIP THEM: (1) the GPT-4o (FT) column reads 3.964 / 3.655 / 2.967 against o3-mini's 3.964 / 3.656 / 2.968 -- identical to within 0.001 on all three rows, which is anomalous enough that ONLY the GPT-4o-vs-o3-mini contrast is cited here and a future G2 should re-pull those two columns specifically before the FT column is used for anything; (2) these rubric scores come from a single verbatim pull (cycle 15) and have not been independently re-pulled, unlike the four TTP rows from the same table which have been confirmed twice; (3) a 1-5 drafting rubric is not commensurable with CTIBench's plausible-vs-correct percentages, so this corroborates direction, not magnitude. Status is deliberately 'proposed' rather than 'supported' for reasons (1) and (2).

issues.title: Is 'AI-generated CTI reliability' a single property, or does it vary sharply by task type (mechanical extraction vs. open-ended reasoning)?
open_questions: SPLIT NOTE (cycle 16, T2, discharging carry-forward [1] after it was carried unactioned for nine consecutive cycles). This issue now covers ONLY the narrow claim: that AI-generated CTI reliability varies sharply by sub-task rather than being a single uniform property. The SPECIFIC ORDINAL AXIS ('mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation'), together with the cycle-2 proposed cross-source synthesis that carried it and the open question about whether a better explanatory variable exists, was MOVED VERBATIM to the new issue 'extraction-vs-reasoning-ordinal-axis'. The reason for the split is that the two claims have very different evidential status and were sharing one issue and one candidate_resolution from cycle 2 to cycle 15, which is exactly why no T4 could score either honestly: the narrow claim has five independent supporting sources (src-0001, src-0002, src-0006, src-0007, and now src-0013 on the calibration axis) while the ordinal axis is actively disputed between src-0006 and src-0007. Do NOT re-merge them.

src-0006's causal-intervention mitigations raised an attribution-adjacent task (Threat Actor Linking) by only +0.055 accuracy, a much smaller gain than LANCE's ~72-86%->97.6% F1 jump on IoC extraction (src-0003) -- but the two are not a controlled comparison (different tasks, metrics, mitigation types: automated retrieval/inference intervention vs. human-in-the-loop regex+LLM pipeline). No source yet tests a LANCE-style human-validated pipeline specifically on ATT&CK mapping or attribution; a search this cycle for such a study (and for RAM/src-2502.02337, an automated non-human-in-the-loop ATT&CK mapper) found none. Does human-in-the-loop validation specifically (not just any targeted mitigation) transfer to reasoning-heavy tasks, and if so how much of the IoC-extraction gain would it recover?

Since src-0003's strong result is single-study/in-house, would the task-dependence conclusion survive an independent replication showing a smaller IoC-extraction advantage? A cycle-6 search for independent LANCE/PRISM replication or critique found none published yet.

candidate_resolutions.summary: The core, narrower claim -- that AI-generated CTI reliability is genuinely task-dependent rather than a single uniform property -- is now supported, not just proposed: src-0006 (cycle 6) directly measures reliability across multiple distinct CTI sub-tasks within one consistent study design (rather than only via cross-benchmark synthesis across different teams/models) and finds F1/AUC ranging roughly 0.20-0.90 by specific sub-task, corroborating the cross-study pattern already visible in src-0001/0002/0003/0005. However, the SPECIFIC ordinal axis proposed above (mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation) is not confirmed by this evidence and is likely too coarse: src-0006 found its failure patterns cut across all 4 CTI pipeline stages it defines, including extraction/contextualization-type tasks, rather than concentrating in 'reasoning' stages. So: task-dependence itself = supported; the specific extraction-vs-reasoning explanatory axis = open, and now positively questioned rather than merely unverified.

ADDED cycle 16 by T2 at the split. Two further within-study measurements strengthen the NARROW claim -- that CTI reliability varies sharply by sub-task rather than being one uniform property -- and both are of the strongest available kind, holding team, corpus, models and harness constant and varying only the sub-task. (1) src-0007: on one expert-annotated corpus drawn from a real company's CTI workflow, the same four models reach IoC-extraction precision 0.8240-0.8846 while scoring 0.2787/0.2270 (GPT-4o) and 0.3480/0.1759 (o3-mini) precision/recall on MITRE ATT&CK TTP identification, and GPT-4o scores 1.140 out of 5 on the threat-actor Attribution rubric against 3.612 out of 5 for root-cause content in the same table -- roughly a 3x spread across sub-tasks with everything else held constant. (2) src-0013 extends task-dependence to a NEW AXIS that no prior source in this base had tested: reliability varies by sub-task not only in accuracy but in CALIBRATION. Within one study, functional calibration is consistently worse than security calibration for every model tested (delta ECE -0.15/-0.16 GPT-4o-mini, -0.26/-0.27 Gemini-2.0-Flash, -0.52/-0.53 Qwen3-Coder-Next). SCOPE LIMIT ON (2), do not strip it: src-0013 measures secure code generation, not CTI, so it corroborates the SHAPE of task-dependence on a security-adjacent task rather than replicating it on CTI material -- see the cycle-16 scope ruling recorded in 'consistency-calibration-as-failure-mode', which declines to treat security-adjacent corroboration as CTI multi-source support. PROVENANCE ASYMMETRY: src-0007's figures were re-verified verbatim by cycle 15's G2 and are exact to four decimal places; src-0013's are single-pass fetches whose results tables have never been pulled whole (carry-forward [20]). This candidate supports TASK-DEPENDENCE ONLY and deliberately takes no position on the ordinal ranking of sub-tasks, which was moved out of this issue to 'extraction-vs-reasoning-ordinal-axis' at the cycle-16 split.

issues.title: Is there a valid ordinal difficulty ranking across CTI sub-tasks (mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation), or is the extraction-vs-reasoning binary too coarse to explain where reliability breaks down?
open_questions: CYCLE-18 HEADLINE, and it changes what this issue is asking. The commensurable measurement that the 'WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE THIS' question below demanded ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS KNOWLEDGE BASE and has since cycle 6: src-0006's Table 2 contains nine rows all reported in F1, over ONE corpus and ONE 15-model set (printed column order G5, Go4, CLD, GEM, LL70, MIX, QWN, GRK, FSC, CB0, ZYS, LLY, CBS, SPT, DHT; 8 general-purpose then 7 cybersecurity-specialised), spanning both ends of the proposed ordering. Restricted to those nine rows the yardstick does not change between sub-tasks, which is exactly the property src-0007 lacks. The table was pulled whole and recomputed at cycle 17, then pulled again from a second URL form and recomputed independently at cycle 18 -- cycle 17's state edits were reverted by the validator, so cycle 18 is the first time this finding has landed. THE ORDERING IS NOT REPRODUCED. Mean F1 across all 15 models, Contextualization ('extraction') stage: IOC Normalization 0.656, Affected Systems 0.650, Attack Infrastructure 0.631, Malware Family Mapping 0.607, stage mean 0.636. Attribution ('reasoning') stage: TTP Extraction 0.673, Infrastructure Reuse 0.612, Relation Graph Building 0.610, False Flag Detection 0.511, stage mean 0.602. Stage gap 0.034 F1 -- about one fifth of the within-Attribution spread (0.511-0.673) and about one eighth of the mean between-model spread on a single task (0.272). The single BEST task in the whole commensurable subset is TTP Extraction at 0.673, an Attribution-stage task, outscoring every Contextualization task including IOC Normalization: the predicted ordering is not merely weak, it is locally inverted at its strongest predicted point. WHAT IS NOW OPEN: (a) does a 0.034 stage gap survive a SECOND commensurable multi-sub-task study; (b) is 0.034 distinguishable from zero at all, given that src-0006 reports no confidence intervals, no seeds and no repeat runs, so this issue cannot presently attach an uncertainty to its own headline number; (c) src-0006's stage labels are the paper's own four-stage pipeline taxonomy and 'Contextualization' is a looser construct than 'mechanical extraction', so a future cycle should test whether re-labelling the nine tasks by output-label-space size rather than by pipeline stage produces a cleaner split.

NEW cycle 18, and it is the strongest replacement hypothesis on the table. On the same nine-row commensurable F1 subset of src-0006's Table 2, the mean BETWEEN-MODEL range within a task is 0.272 (Affected Systems 0.464, False Flag Detection 0.393, Attack Infrastructure 0.371, Patch Recommendation 0.276, TTP Extraction 0.273, Infrastructure Reuse 0.226, Malware Family Mapping 0.155, Relation Graph Building 0.155, IOC Normalization 0.132) and the mean BETWEEN-TASK range within a model is 0.263 (from 0.171 for ZYS up to 0.404 for LL70 and 0.403 for LLY). EQUAL TO WITHIN 0.009. That answers the last inherited open_question below in the affirmative and mis-specifies the axis: task identity is not the dominant explanatory variable, model identity is at least its equal. A further and weaker signal points at CORPUS identity: the same nominal sub-task, ATT&CK TTP mapping, scores F1 0.478-0.751 in src-0006 but a derived F1 of 0.157-0.250 in src-0007 -- a shift of roughly 0.4 on ONE task, larger than any between-task gap either paper reports. That comparison is uncontrolled (task definition, model set, publication year and metric decomposition all differ at once) and is recorded as a lead, not a result. STILL OPEN: is there any study that varies task while holding model fixed and varies model while holding task fixed, reporting variance components rather than leaving them to a reader's arithmetic? No source in this base does.

NEW cycle 18, and it is a caveat on this issue's own headline evidence rather than a question about CTI. Four of the nine commensurable F1 rows in src-0006's Table 2 -- IOC Normalization, Malware Family Mapping, Relation Graph Building, Infrastructure Reuse -- are STRICTLY MONOTONE DECREASING across all eight general-purpose model columns in exactly the printed column order, with unusually smooth decrements. For independent measurements the chance of one row matching a fixed eight-column order is 1/8! = about 1 in 40,320. Cycle 17 counted eleven such rows across all twenty-eight rows of the table and re-pulled ten of them from a second URL form with an explicit instruction to answer 'CANNOT READ' rather than reconstruct; they returned identical cell for cell. Cycle 18 pulled the nine F1 rows again and independently reproduced every cell and every derived mean. So the pattern is as-printed in the paper and is NOT a fetch artefact; its cause is unknown and no cycle should guess at one. It matters because src-0006 is cited by three issues. The cycle-18 headline is deliberately robust to it: dropping all four monotone rows leaves Contextualization 0.641 against Attribution 0.592, gap 0.049, same direction, TTP Extraction still the highest single task. SEPARATELY, AND NOW CONFIRMED BY TWO CYCLES: src-0006's stored key_claim describes 'Infrastructure Reuse peaks at F1 0.754 for a specialized agent vs. 0.688 for a general model', but the 0.688 column is ZYS, which sits inside the paper's cyber-specialised block; the general-purpose peak on that row is G5 at 0.677. The comparison's direction survives, the label does not. A corrective key_claim was APPENDED to src-0006's entry in state/knowledge/index.json at cycle 18 -- nothing was deleted or rewritten -- and state/knowledge/src-0006.md was left untouched.

ANSWERED IN PART BY CYCLE 18, kept verbatim because its closing question is still live. Its premise 'reliability ranging F1/AUC ~0.20-0.90' is loose and is corrected above: the true F1 span of the nine commensurable rows is 0.286 (False Flag Detection, LLY) to 0.882 (Affected Systems, LL70). Its closing question -- is there a better explanatory variable than a coarse extraction-vs-reasoning binary -- now has a candidate answer, model identity, entered as a proposed candidate_resolution below. ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. MOVED HERE VERBATIM from 'task-dependent-reliability-framing' at the cycle-16 split; originally written by cycle 6. The cross-cutting 'mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation' ordinal axis is not confirmed and is now positively in doubt: src-0006 (cycle 6), the first source to measure multiple distinct CTI sub-tasks within one consistent study, found its 3 failure patterns (spurious correlations, contradictory knowledge, constrained generalization) occur across all 4 pipeline stages it defines, including 'contextualization'-type tasks that would loosely be called extraction, with reliability ranging F1/AUC ~0.20-0.90 by specific sub-task rather than cleanly by extraction-vs-reasoning category. Is there a better explanatory variable (e.g. heterogeneity/volatility/ambiguity of the specific task's input data, or the size/discreteness of its output label space) than a coarse extraction-vs-reasoning binary?

CYCLE-18 NOTE, prepended not substituted. I re-examined this pair with src-0006's Table 2 in hand and STILL DECLINE to open a G3 contradiction, for the cycle-10 reason endorsed by cycle 16 and repeated verbatim below. What cycle 18 adds is that src-0007's ordinal reading, stated below as fact, does not survive src-0007's own table: the third rung depends entirely on an unstated normalisation of a 1-5 rubric -- GPT-4o's 1.140/5 becomes 0.228 under x/5 or 0.035 under (x-1)/4, against a derived TTP F1 of 0.2502, so attribution either ties classification or is seven times worse -- and the middle-to-third rung ORDERING REVERSES BETWEEN TWO MODELS IN THE SAME TABLE, since o3-mini's 2.968/5 is 0.594 or 0.492, both ABOVE its derived TTP F1 of 0.2337. The SUPPORTS half of the tension below is therefore weaker than it reads. That is a reason to doubt src-0007's ordinal reading, not a reason to declare the two sources in conflict. (Provenance note for a future cycle: the rubric values 1.140 and 2.968 come from cycle 15's verbatim whole-table pull of src-0007's Table 4 and were re-checked at cycle 16, but they are NOT recorded in state/knowledge/src-0007.md, which notes those rows only as existing. They are traceable to src-0007 through the cycle-15 log.) ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. THE CENTRAL TENSION, and why NO contradiction entry was opened -- restated in full at the cycle-16 split so that no future cycle re-litigates it from scratch. src-0007's Table 4 SUPPORTS an ordinal reading: on one corpus with one model set, IoC extraction precision is 0.8240-0.8846, ATT&CK TTP identification precision is 0.2787-0.3480, and the threat-actor Attribution rubric score for GPT-4o is 1.140 out of 5 -- mechanical extraction above technique mapping above attribution, which is the ordering the axis predicts. src-0006's Table 5 OPPOSES it: its failure subtypes span all four pipeline stages it defines, e.g. 'Co-mention bias (Type 1.1) -- stages 1234', so the failure MECHANISMS do not respect the ordering. Cycle 10 examined this pair and DECLINED to open a G3 contradiction, reasoning that src-0006 measures where failure mechanisms OCCUR while src-0007 measures where performance LEVELS differ, and that these are compatible rather than conflicting. Cycle 16 re-read both and did NOT overturn that reasoning: a failure mechanism can be present at every pipeline stage while its impact on measured performance is unequal across those stages, and both facts can hold simultaneously. That is precisely why this is an OPEN ISSUE and not a contradiction -- the two sources are not in conflict; the AXIS is simply not established by either of them.

SUPERSEDED BY CYCLE 18, kept verbatim because its commensurability standard is the right standard and cycle 18 met it, not because the question is still open. The bar it sets was cleared by src-0006's Table 2, which cycle 16 did not know contained nine same-metric rows. Its closing instruction -- 'until a commensurable cross-sub-task measurement exists, this issue should not rise above proposed' -- is therefore DISCHARGED and no longer binds a T4. One half of it survives as a finding rather than a question: the commensurability objection FAILS for the extraction-vs-classification rung of src-0007 and HOLDS for the third rung. Solving 2PR/(P+R) for the unreported IoC recall at which each model's IoC F1 would fall to its own derived TTP F1 gives crossovers of 0.1475 (GPT-4o), 0.1354 (o3-mini), 0.1180 (GPT-4o FT) and 0.0887 (GPT-4o-mini FT), every one BELOW that same model's actual TTP recall of 0.2270, 0.1759, 0.1846 and 0.1414 respectively. So if IoC recall were merely as bad as TTP recall, the gap survives for all four models; it breaks only if IoC recall is worse than TTP recall by a further factor of 1.3-1.6, i.e. an absolute recall of 0.09-0.15, which no source in this base reports for report-level extraction. The precision-only omission is a real reporting defect and is NOT an explanation of src-0007's extraction-vs-TTP gap. ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE THIS (cycle 16): a single study measuring ONE commensurable metric across sub-tasks spanning the full proposed ordering, on ONE corpus with ONE model set. src-0007 comes closest and still falls short, because its yardstick changes between rows -- IoC extraction reports precision only (no recall, no F1, and the paper gives no reason for the omission, a fact cycle 15's whole-table pull confirmed is real rather than a fetch artefact), TTP identification reports precision and recall, and drafting reports a 1-5 rubric. Its apparent ordering is therefore partly an artefact of changing the measurement instrument between sub-tasks. Until a commensurable cross-sub-task measurement exists, this issue should not rise above 'proposed'.

ANSWERED BY CYCLE 18, in the affirmative -- see the between-model-versus-between-task entry above (0.272 against 0.263, equal to within 0.009). The AUC 0.912-versus-0.547 pair this question cites was re-verified exact at cycle 17 and is an instance of the pattern rather than an outlier. Kept verbatim because it is the question that turned out to matter most. ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. Does the ordering, if it holds at all, hold WITHIN a stage as well as between stages? src-0006 reports F1/AUC ~0.20-0.90 across tasks and models including a spread as wide as AUC 0.912 vs 0.547 for two different models on the SAME task (Source Reliability Scoring). If between-model variance on one task is comparable to between-task variance, then task identity is not the dominant explanatory variable and the axis is mis-specified regardless of which way the between-task comparison comes out.

candidate_resolutions.summary: MOVED VERBATIM from 'task-dependent-reliability-framing' at the cycle-16 T2 split; this text was originally written by cycle 2 and its status of 'proposed' is carried over unchanged. It is reproduced here rather than rewritten, and it is the ordinal-axis half of what was previously one conflated issue. ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. Across the 5 collected sources, reliability of AI-generated CTI is strongly task-dependent rather than a uniform property: narrow, mechanical extraction (IoC extraction, src-0003) reaches near-97% F1 when LLM output is constrained and human-validated, while open-ended reasoning tasks (ATT&CK technique mapping, threat-actor attribution, general threat-intel reasoning: src-0001, src-0002, src-0005) remain unreliable (accuracy ceilings around 52-72%, confidence miscalibration, and plausible-but-wrong outputs) even as model scale increases. This framing is a synthesis of currently-available evidence, not itself directly measured by any single source, and should be treated as a working hypothesis pending the open questions above. CYCLE-16 ANNOTATION, appended not substituted: the part of this text that survives the split into the parent issue is task-dependence itself, which is now supported there by five sources. What remains HERE and remains merely proposed is the ORDERING -- the claim that the extraction-vs-reasoning distinction is what explains the spread. Note also that the strongest number in this text, src-0003's 97.6% F1, is itself one side of the open contradiction ctr-0001, in which src-0007 measures an unscaffolded LLM at 0.82-0.88 precision on the same broad task; if ctr-0001 resolves in favour of the scaffolding explanation, then the top of this proposed ordering is measuring pipeline design rather than task difficulty, and the axis loses its clearest supporting datapoint. CYCLE-18 REJECTION, appended not substituted; the cycle-16 annotation and the original cycle-2 text above are preserved word for word and the provenance header stands. STATUS CHANGED FROM 'proposed' TO 'rejected'. What is rejected is the ORDINAL AXIS ONLY -- the claim that a mechanical-extraction-versus-open-ended-reasoning distinction is what explains the spread in CTI reliability. Task-dependence itself is NOT rejected; it lives, supported by five sources, in the parent issue 'task-dependent-reliability-framing'. REASON: the one commensurable within-study measurement in this knowledge base, src-0006's Table 2 restricted to its nine F1 rows over one corpus and 15 models, puts the Attribution stage only 0.034 F1 below the Contextualization stage while making an Attribution-stage task -- TTP Extraction at 0.673 -- the best-performing task in the entire subset; and src-0007, the source whose numbers this text leans on for the reasoning end, orders its own middle and third rungs OPPOSITELY for GPT-4o and o3-mini, on a rubric normalisation the paper never states. An ordering that is locally inverted at its strongest predicted point in one study, and that reverses between two models of the same family in another, is not a property of the tasks. See this issue's open_questions for the full derivation and its three caveats.

SUPPORTED, entered cycle 18. The identical finding was produced by cycle 17, whose state edits the validator reverted; cycle 18 re-pulled src-0006's Table 2 from a second URL form and re-derived every mean, range and crossover independently before landing it. THE CLAIM: the proposed ordinal axis 'mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation' is NOT supported by the only commensurable cross-sub-task measurement available in this base, and the extraction-versus-reasoning binary is too coarse to explain where CTI reliability breaks down. TWO INDEPENDENT ROUTES, from two unaffiliated teams on two corpora with two disjoint model sets. (1) src-0006's Table 2 restricted to its nine F1 rows -- one corpus, one 15-model set, one metric -- gives a Contextualization stage mean of 0.636 (IOC Normalization 0.656, Affected Systems 0.650, Attack Infrastructure 0.631, Malware Family Mapping 0.607) against an Attribution stage mean of 0.602 (TTP Extraction 0.673, Infrastructure Reuse 0.612, Relation Graph Building 0.610, False Flag Detection 0.511). The 0.034 gap is in the predicted direction but is roughly one eighth of the 0.272 mean between-model spread on a single task, and the best task in the subset is an Attribution-stage task. (2) src-0007's Table 4, the source that appears to support the ordering, reverses its own middle-to-third rung between two models: GPT-4o's attribution rubric of 1.140/5 normalises to 0.228 or 0.035 against a derived TTP F1 of 0.2502 (at or below), while o3-mini's 2.968/5 normalises to 0.594 or 0.492 against 0.2337 (above), under both defensible normalisations. THREE MATERIAL CAVEATS. (a) src-0006 reports no confidence intervals, no seeds and no repeat runs, so 0.034 carries no uncertainty estimate; this candidate asserts that the ordering is NOT SUPPORTED, not that the reverse ordering holds. (b) Four of the nine rows are strictly monotone decreasing across all eight general-purpose columns in printed order, a pattern of unknown cause verified as-printed by three pulls across two URL forms; dropping all four leaves 0.641 against 0.592, gap 0.049, same direction, same best task. (c) The fourth rung of the proposed ordering, open-ended GENERATION, is not represented in the commensurable subset at all, so this candidate refutes the extraction-versus-classification-versus-attribution part of the ordering and is SILENT on generation, which remains supported in the parent issue by src-0001's extraction-versus-generation confidence-interval-width split of 0.02 against 0.06.

PROPOSED, entered cycle 18 as the replacement explanatory variable this issue's inherited first open_question asked for. THE CLAIM: model identity explains as much of the variance in CTI sub-task reliability as sub-task identity does, corpus identity may explain more than either, and the extraction-versus-reasoning category is a weak third. On src-0006's nine-row commensurable F1 subset the mean between-model range within a task is 0.272 and the mean between-task range within a model is 0.263 -- equal to within 0.009 -- while the extraction-versus-reasoning stage gap on those same rows is 0.034. Separately, the same nominal sub-task, ATT&CK TTP mapping, scores F1 0.478-0.751 in src-0006 against a derived F1 of 0.157-0.250 in src-0007: a shift of roughly 0.4 on one task, larger than any between-task gap either paper reports. THREE OBJECTIONS TO ITSELF, which is why this is proposed and not supported. (i) The between-model and between-task figures are RANGES, not variance components; a range is sensitive to a single outlying model, and src-0006's LLY is an outlier on two of the nine rows (False Flag Detection 0.286, Patch Recommendation 0.442). (ii) The cross-source TTP comparison is uncontrolled -- task definition, model set, publication year and metric decomposition all differ at once -- so corpus identity is only one of at least four candidate explanations for that 0.4 shift. (iii) Both figures come from ONE study's table, and no cycle has checked whether the same equality holds in any other multi-model multi-task security evaluation; src-0014's roughly fourfold spread in prompt-sensitivity between models on identical data introduces a fourth variable, prompt strategy, that this candidate does not account for at all.

issues.title: Have AI-generated CTI failures already reached production/publication at real institutions, and how do institutions respond when caught?
open_questions: REWRITTEN cycle 12, and deliberately reframed so it stops being answerable by anecdote. The base rate of hallucinated citations across CTI PUBLISHERS is still unmeasured and no cycle should claim otherwise: we now have two named incidents (ENISA src-0004, EY Canada src-0012), and two anecdotes are not a rate. What was found instead is the nearest systematic audit in an ADJACENT population -- src-0011 (GhostCite) manually verified 2.2M citations across 56,381 papers and reports 1.01% of papers at Security venues containing at least one invalid citation. It cannot be transferred to CTI: it audits peer-reviewed conference papers, defines a ghost citation as one absent from academic databases (inapplicable to CTI footnotes, which are news/vendor URLs), and reports per-PAPER rates that are not comparable with src-0004's per-FOOTNOTE 26/492. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE THIS: (a) a link-resolution/footnote-verification sweep over N published threat reports from M agencies and vendors, which is mechanically cheap since both known incidents were found precisely this way (dead links); (b) a disclosure-policy survey of CTI publishers; or (c) an existing audit of vendor/agency reports if one can be found. Cycle 12 searched for (c) and found only academic-corpus and consulting-report audits, never a CTI-publisher audit.

PARTIALLY ANSWERED cycle 12, first half CLOSED. ENISA's AI usage was NOT disclosed to readers before publication and was admitted only when Der Spiegel asked after external researchers found the dead links (src-0004). Stronger now: ENISA's own publication pages for BOTH affected reports (src-0009, src-0010) carry revision notices dated 09 January 2026 describing the fix purely mechanically -- 'updated to edit some links' and 'updated to correct some broken links and typos' -- and as of 2026-07-29, roughly 8 months after exposure, NEITHER page carries any mention of AI or generative AI. So the non-disclosure was not merely pre-publication; it persists in the corrected record. STILL OPEN: whether ENISA changed any internal policy (a cycle-12 search found no published policy change), and whether any peer agency changed disclosure policy in response. Also still open at PDF level: the front matter / legal notice of the v1.2 PDFs was not pulled, so the 'no AI disclosure anywhere' claim is currently established only for the landing pages.

PARTIALLY ANSWERED cycle 12, and the answer for the NUMBER is no. ENISA's own primary artefacts (src-0009, src-0010) independently corroborate the STRUCTURE of the incident -- two reports, published October 1 and November 6 2025, both revised on 09 January 2026, both revisions concerning links -- exactly as src-0004 reports secondhand. But neither ENISA page gives any footnote count and neither mentions AI, so the 26-of-492 figure remains sourced to Der Spiegel via Heise and is corroborated only by outlets (cybernews, Tagesspiegel, derStandard) that themselves cite Der Spiegel, i.e. NOT independently. NOTE FOR FUTURE CYCLES: Der Spiegel's original article could not be retrieved -- spiegel.de is blocked to this agent's user agent (WebSearch returns HTTP 400 'domains are not accessible to our user agent'), so this is an infrastructure limit, not an unsearched direction; do not burn budget retrying it the same way. The remaining routes to the number are counting the footnotes in the archived v1.1/original PDF against v1.2, or locating Prof. Christian Dietrich's / Institut fuer Internet-Sicherheit's own writeup. ENISA's silence is NOT a contradiction of src-0004 and no G3 entry was opened: the notices assign no cause at all rather than a competing one.

NEW cycle 12. Institutional responses to the SAME failure mode diverged sharply -- EY Canada withdrew the offending report entirely and issued a statement invoking its 'organisation-wide commitment to the responsible use of AI' (src-0012), while ENISA retained both reports, patched the links, and described the correction without reference to AI (src-0009, src-0010). What predicts which response an institution gives: commercial reputational exposure vs public-mandate insulation, the presence of a named external investigator, the share of citations affected (16/27 = 59% for EY vs 26/492 = 5% for ENISA), or something else? Two cases cannot distinguish these; more incidents with recorded responses would.

NEW cycle 12. BOTH known incidents were discovered from the outside by parties clicking through footnotes (Westfaelische Hochschule researchers for ENISA, GPTZero for EY), and in neither case did the publisher's internal QA catch it. src-0011 supplies a measured analogue of why in academic publishing (76.7% of surveyed reviewers do not thoroughly check references; 80.0% never suspect fake citations). Does ANY CTI publisher run automated link-resolution or citation-verification on reports before release, and is there a single documented case of this failure mode being caught internally? No source in the base documents one.

candidate_resolutions.summary: At least one major institutional CTI publisher (ENISA, the EU's cybersecurity agency) published AI-hallucinated citations in production threat-landscape reports (Oct/Nov 2025), including a technical fingerprint (misattributing the name 'APT29' to Microsoft's naming convention, when Microsoft actually uses 'Midnight Blizzard') consistent with LLM-generated text. The failure was caught by external academic researchers checking footnote links, not by internal QA, and the agency's public response ('human errors') did not fully acknowledge AI attribution even after exposure. This establishes existence of the failure mode in production but not its frequency/base rate across the CTI industry.

ADDED cycle 12. The ENISA incident is no longer carried by a single secondary source. ENISA's own publication pages for both named reports independently corroborate the incident's verifiable structure: 'ENISA Threat Landscape 2025' (published 1 Oct 2025) carries 'Revision Notice - Version 1.2. (09 January 2026): This publication has been updated to edit some links.' and the sectorial 'Public Administration' report (published 6 Nov 2025) carries 'Revision Notice - Version 1.2 (09 January 2026): This publication has been updated to correct some broken links and typos.' Two reports, October and November 2025, both corrected for links on the same January 2026 date -- matching src-0004's secondhand account on report count, dates and defect type. What ENISA's own record does NOT contain is any footnote count and any mention of AI, so the 26/492 figure and the AI attribution remain dependent on Der Spiegel via Heise.

ADDED cycle 12. The failure mode RECURS across institution types and is not an ENISA idiosyncrasy. EY Canada's 2025 report 'Points of Attack: Uncovering Cyber Threats and Fraud in Loyalty Systems' was found by GPTZero (14 May 2026) to have 16 of 27 references hallucinated, with 'more than a half-dozen footnotes led to dead webpages or did not contain the cited information'; EY Canada removed the study from its website. This is a commercial Big Four publisher of security/fraud content, discovered by the same route as ENISA (an outside party clicking through footnotes) roughly six months later. Two independent institutions, one public and one commercial, is materially stronger than one for the EXISTENCE and RECURRENCE claim -- and still says nothing about frequency. Scope note: loyalty-systems fraud is security-adjacent published content, not threat intelligence in the narrow IoC/TTP/attribution sense measured elsewhere in this knowledge base.

ADDED cycle 12. On the issue's second question -- how institutions respond when caught -- the two documented cases diverge, so there is no single institutional response pattern to report. EY Canada WITHDREW the report and issued a statement referencing accuracy and 'an organisation-wide commitment to the responsible use of AI', saying it was reviewing why the study was published. ENISA RETAINED both reports, issued v1.2 corrections describing only link edits and typos, characterised the underlying errors to the press as 'human errors' while confirming AI was permitted for 'minor editorial revisions', and as of 2026-07-29 carries no AI disclosure on either publication page. The common element across both is that neither institution's internal QA detected the problem and both were corrected only after external publication of the finding.

ADDED cycle 12, status PROPOSED and deliberately not promoted -- read the scope limit before citing. No base rate for hallucinated citations in CTI publications exists. The closest systematic measurement is src-0011 (GhostCite), which manually verified a flagged subset of 2.2M citations across 56,381 papers at top AI/ML and Security venues (2020-2025) and found 1.07% of papers overall, and 1.01% of papers at Security venues, containing at least one invalid or fabricated citation, with an 80.9% increase in 2025 alone and the authors calling their figure 'a conservative lower bound'. This is NOT the CTI rate and must not be quoted as one: different population (peer-reviewed conference papers, which have reviewers; CTI reports have none), different citation ecology (academic references vs news/vendor URLs), and different denominator (per-paper vs src-0004's per-footnote 26/492). What it does support is a directional claim -- that fabricated citations survive into refereed security literature at a nonzero and rising rate despite peer review -- which makes it implausible that unrefereed CTI publishing is cleaner. That inference is the proposed part, and no source tests it.

issues.title: Do LLM-based security triage and response systems fail by accepting or acting on far too much -- an under-refusal failure that accuracy-based evaluation does not detect?
open_questions: IS OVER-ACCEPTANCE A PROPERTY OF THE MODELS OR OF THE HARNESS? This is the issue's central unknown and neither source addresses it. Neither src-0007 nor src-0015 varies the decision threshold, the stated cost of a false positive in the prompt, the availability of an explicit abstain option, or the presence of a human confirmation step. src-0003 established for a different sub-task (IoC extraction) that scaffolding around the model can dominate measured reliability; the analogous experiment for triage -- does an explicit abstain option, a stated false-positive cost, or a required evidence-fetch step move precision (Accepted) off 0.27-0.40 -- has not been run by any source in this base. Until it is, 'the models under-refuse' and 'these harnesses were built with no refusal affordance' are indistinguishable.

WHAT IS THE OPERATIONAL COST, and is it actually worse than the status quo? Neither source converts its false-positive rate into analyst hours, containment blast radius, or alert-fatigue effects, so precision (Accepted) of 0.27 cannot yet be compared against human triage on any common currency. Note a structural obstacle: src-0007's ground truth IS the human analyst's accept/reject decision, so by construction it carries no human error bar and cannot tell us whether human triage would score better on its own benchmark.

MERGED IN FROM carry-forward [15] at the cycle-16 split decision; cycle 12 excluded this from the knowledge base as a source and cycle 16 judges it belongs HERE, as an open question rather than as evidence. The mirror image of automated over-acceptance is AI-generated security claims arriving INBOUND in volume: curl ended its HackerOne bug bounty on 31 January 2026 after a flood of AI-generated 'slop' vulnerability reports, with reported figures of roughly 20% of submissions being AI slop by mid-2025 and the confirmed-vulnerability rate falling from about 15% historically to under 5%. 'AI slop arrives inbound AND automated triage cannot filter it' is a coherent single problem that this issue and carry-forward [15] describe better jointly than either does alone -- and it has a sharp practical edge, because if automated triage accepts 60-73% of what human analysts reject, it is precisely the wrong instrument for the volume problem it is most often proposed to solve. THIS IS NOT YET EVIDENCE AND MUST NOT BE CITED AS SUCH: no curl/HackerOne source exists in state/knowledge/index.json and a T2 must not invent sources (G1). A future T1 should collect it, reported at bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/curl-ending-bug-bounty-program-after-flood-of-ai-slop-reports/. Until collected, this is a question, not a claim.

Does the under-refusal generalise to the CTI sub-tasks measured elsewhere in this base? If a model were asked to extract IoCs or map ATT&CK techniques with an explicit 'insufficient evidence' option available, would it use it? src-0014 supplies this base's only abstention data -- self-consistency collapsing coverage to 24.04-60.85% -- but on vulnerability detection rather than CTI, and it measures abstention INDUCED by sampling disagreement rather than abstention OFFERED as a choice, so it does not answer this.

Is there a trade-off frontier, or is this simply a badly-set threshold? src-0007's recall (Accepted) of 0.90-1.00 alongside precision of 0.27-0.40 is consistent with a threshold set to maximise recall; nobody has published the precision the same models reach at a recall of, say, 0.7. If the frontier is favourable, this is a tuning problem and largely solved; if precision stays low across the whole frontier, it is a capability problem. No source in this base reports a precision-recall curve for triage.

candidate_resolutions.summary: CREATED cycle 16 by T2, discharging carry-forward [3] and merging carry-forward [15]; six cycles elapsed between the first proposal of this issue and the first cycle with standing to create it. Two independent sources -- different teams, different task framings, different model generations, different years -- find the same failure: the decision threshold is set so permissively that the system accepts or acts on most of what a human analyst would reject. src-0007 (CyberThreat-Eval; Microsoft Research/Microsoft/HKUST, Mar 2026) measures automated triage on a real company's daily CTI workflow and reports an extreme asymmetry, recall (Accepted) 0.90-1.00 against precision (Accepted) 0.27-0.40 across all four models tested. src-0015 (OpenSec, Jan 2026) measures frontier incident-response agents over 40 episodes per model and finds GPT-5.2 containing in 100% of episodes at an 82.5% false-positive rate, DeepSeek 3.2 92.5% at 65%, Gemini 3 75% at 57.5%, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 62.5% at 45%, with an evidence-gated action rate of only 0.375-0.542 -- every model acts without first fetching trusted evidence about the target entity on a majority or near-majority of its containment actions. WHY THIS IS AN ISSUE AND NOT A FOOTNOTE UNDER ACCURACY: src-0015 locates the defect precisely, stating that 'All models correctly identify the ground-truth threat when they act; the calibration gap is not in detection but in restraint.' Detection accuracy is fine. These systems would be scored WELL by essentially every metric used elsewhere in this knowledge base, and the defect is invisible to all of them -- which is exactly the argument for giving it its own issue rather than filing it under an existing accuracy-shaped one. PROVENANCE ASYMMETRY, do not flatten it: src-0007 is institutionally affiliated, methodologically detailed, and had all nine of its stored Table 4 rows re-verified verbatim by cycle 15's G2 exact to four decimal places; src-0015 is by its own recorded assessment the weakest-provenance source in this base -- single-author preprint filed cs.AI, no stated venue, peer review or affiliation, n=40 synthetic RL-seed episodes per model with no confidence intervals, and only the GPT-5.2-versus-Sonnet-4.5 contrast robust, with the middle two models' ordering unresolved. The claim therefore RESTS on src-0007; src-0015 corroborates its direction on a different task and a newer model generation, which is worth a great deal for showing the failure is not one benchmark's artefact, and is worth little as independent quantification. ONE POOLING ERROR TO AVOID: src-0015's 'calibration' is an action-threshold construct (false-positive rate, evidence-gating), NOT the ECE/Brier confidence calibration of src-0001 and src-0013, and the two must never be averaged or quoted as the same measurement.

contradictions.description: MAGNITUDE CONFLICT on how reliable LLM-based IoC extraction from real-world threat material actually is. src-0003 (LANCE/PRISM, arXiv 2506.11325): 97.6% overall F1 against a manually-validated 1,791-IoC benchmark, with the best legacy baseline at 86% (VirusTotal@threshold=1). src-0007 (CyberThreat-Eval, arXiv 2603.09452): vanilla-LLM IoC extraction precision 0.8240 (GPT-4o) / 0.8503 (o3-mini) / 0.8846 (GPT-4o FT) / 0.6944 (GPT-4o-mini FT) over 1310 expert-annotated IoCs from a production CTI workflow -- i.e. an unscaffolded LLM lands at or below the level src-0003 assigns to the LEGACY tools it set out to beat. Taken at face value the two sources leave a reader with opposite impressions of whether mechanical IoC extraction is a solved problem. NEITHER SIDE IS PICKED, and this entry deliberately records that the conflict may dissolve on inspection, because three confounds are unresolved: (1) SYSTEM -- LANCE is regex pre-filter + LLM + human validation, src-0007's Table 4 is explicitly headed 'Vanilla LLMs', so this may be a measurement of scaffolding value rather than a disagreement; (2) METRIC -- 97.6% is an F1, 0.82-0.88 are precision with no recall reported anywhere in src-0007 and no reason given for the omission; (3) CORPUS -- PRISM is 50 public threat reports, src-0007's material is an unnamed company's internal daily workflow of unknown relative difficulty. Neither paper cites the other. RESOLUTION PATH for a future cycle: recover recall/F1 from src-0007's released code (GitHub/HuggingFace per its abstract) to make the metrics comparable, and/or find any source running an unscaffolded LLM against PRISM or a LANCE-style scaffolded pipeline against CyberThreat-Eval. If confound (1) is confirmed as the explanation, this contradiction should be closed and its content folded into ioc-extraction-reliability's third candidate_resolution (scaffolding, not the model, sets extraction reliability) rather than left open as a conflict.
